extracted.intended_audience: general readers and historians interested in the history of advertising
extracted.subtask_description: A 19th-century illustrated historical survey of advertising from ancient times through the 18th–19th centuries, compiling anecdotes, specimens, and biographical notes for a general and scholarly readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid untrustworthy statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Little in the way of so-called statistics of modern advertisers will be found in the book, as I fancy it is better to be silent than to make untrustworthy statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorial policy: omit or avoid publishing precise numerical claims about advertisers' annual outlay when they cannot be reliably verified; the author notes firms/managers often do not know exact sums or tend to exaggerate. Prefer silence to uncertain figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make advertisements tell their own story
rubrics_metrics.description: I have endeavoured as much as possible, and wherever practicable, to make the advertisements tell their own story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological guidance: present primary advertisement texts and specimens with minimal editorial overwriting so that examples illustrate historical points directly; where practical, allow original ads to serve as evidence and narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent waste of space / be concise
rubrics_metrics.description: At the same time I have tried hard to prevent waste of space, and so far have, if in no other way, succeeded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial standard: be economical with space—select and present material concisely rather than including redundant or excessive commentary; judicious trimming is a deliberate merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curate selections by informed judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: As far as my judgment has allowed me, I have selected what appeared best; other tastes might lead to other results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curation note: the work is selective and subjective—examples are chosen based on the author's assessment of merit and interest; readers should expect incompleteness and that alternative selections would be reasonable.
